questions.f: When one colleague claims every launch this year hit its date and another claims none did, one of them must be right, because the two claims are contradictories rather than contraries.
questions.x: "All" versus "none" sits on the top side of the square, where both can be false; the truth may be that some launches were on time and some were not. Contradictories, such as "all" versus "some did not", are the pairs where exactly one is true.

questions.t: Boethius's Latin translations and commentaries, written shortly after 500 CE, made the square of opposition a fixture of medieval logic teaching.
questions.f: John Buridan's Latin translations and commentaries, written shortly after 500 CE, made the square of opposition a fixture of medieval logic teaching.
questions.x: Boethius carried the diagram into the Latin West in the early sixth century. Buridan worked much later, in the fourteenth century, and is known for testing the square's rules against empty terms rather than spreading it.

questions.t: A trial of a shorter mobile checkout form looks like a win, but a colleague notes that a payment outage overlapped the test, so the team reruns it. That critical scrutiny is part of the scientific process itself.
questions.f: A trial of a shorter mobile checkout form looks like a win, but a colleague notes that a payment outage overlapped the test, so the team reruns it. That critical scrutiny comes after the scientific process, which ends once the data are analysed.
questions.x: On the realistic picture of science, ideas are kept only if they survive testing and the community's probing, and results are exposed to criticism and replication before anyone relies on them. A step list that stops at analysis leaves out the check that caught the confound here.

questions.t: When judging whether an inquiry is scientific, don't insist on a formal hypothesis up front, since many legitimate scientific methods, such as exploratory data work, proceed without one.
questions.f: When judging whether an inquiry is scientific, insist on a formal hypothesis up front, since exploratory data work without one can't count as a scientific method.
questions.x: Treating hypothesis testing as the only scientific method is a common misconception, even among science teachers. Science uses a plurality of methods, and the useful question is whether the claims end up tested against evidence, not whether a recipe was followed.

questions.t: The step-by-step school recipe for the scientific method (observe, hypothesise, experiment, conclude) is a later teaching device, traced partly to Pearson's 1892 Grammar of Science and Dewey's 1910 How We Think.
questions.f: The step-by-step school recipe for the scientific method (observe, hypothesise, experiment, conclude) comes straight from Francis Bacon's 1620 Novum Organum, which set out those steps.
questions.x: Bacon proposed eliminative induction with tables of presence, absence and degrees, not the classroom step list. The tidy recipe arrived around the turn of the twentieth century, and critics argue it has no canonical source in the history of science.

questions.t: A manager argues the sales team can move to a four-day week because it worked for the similar support team. A colleague replies that engineering tried the same change and missed two release dates. Her reply is a counter-analogy.
questions.f: A manager argues the sales team can move to a four-day week because it worked for the similar support team. A colleague replies that engineering tried the same change and missed two release dates. Her reply points to a relevant difference between sales and support.
questions.x: A counter-analogy brings in a third case that resembles the source but turned out the other way. Pointing to a relevant difference would instead attack the sales-support comparison itself, for example by noting that sales closes deals in Friday meetings.

questions.t: To test an analogy, ask what in the source case actually produced the outcome, then check whether that factor is also present in the target case.
questions.f: To test an analogy, count how many features the two cases share overall, since the sheer number of shared features is the central test of a good analogy.
questions.x: Many shared features can be irrelevant to the conclusion, which is how faulty analogies arise. The stronger test links the outcome to its cause in the source and asks whether nothing in the target blocks that link.

questions.t: In Mary Hesse's layout of an analogy, features not yet known to match or differ between the two cases make up the neutral analogy.
questions.f: In Mary Hesse's layout of an analogy, features not yet known to match or differ between the two cases make up the negative analogy.
questions.x: Hesse sorts features into three groups: known similarities (positive), known differences (negative), and the still-unknown ones (neutral). An argument from analogy projects something from the source into that unknown territory in the target.

questions.t: A support agent's ratings fall for a quarter and her manager decides she has "lost motivation", overlooking that she was moved to the queue for a botched recall where every caller was angry. That is the fundamental attribution error.
questions.f: A support agent's ratings fall for a quarter and her manager decides she has "lost motivation", overlooking that she was moved to the queue for a botched recall where every caller was angry. That is the actor-observer asymmetry.
questions.x: The manager explains another person's behaviour by a trait while missing a situation that fully accounts for it, the core of the fundamental attribution error. The actor-observer asymmetry is a narrower claim contrasting how we explain our own actions with others', which isn't at issue here.

questions.t: To curb the fundamental attribution error in performance reviews, put the situational information in plain view, such as showing a fund's returns against the market in one clear figure.
questions.f: To curb the fundamental attribution error in performance reviews, keep situational information in the background, since putting it in plain view tends to make reviewers overcorrect.
questions.x: In Scopelliti and colleagues' studies, the most bias-prone people ignored situational numbers that were available but buried, and the bias vanished once the comparison was shown in one simple figure. Making the situation easy to see is the fix.

questions.t: Mentally busy observers are more prone to the fundamental attribution error, because the quick trait inference still happens while the effortful correction for the situation gets skipped.
questions.f: Mentally busy observers are less prone to the fundamental attribution error, because the effortful trait inference gets skipped while the quick correction for the situation still happens.
questions.x: On the characterization-correction account, people first read a trait off the behaviour automatically, then adjust for circumstances only if they have the capacity. Cognitive load knocks out that second step, so judging people while rushed is a warning sign.

questions.t: A consultant recommends a software platform and is paid a referral fee by its vendor, though nothing suggests the fee swayed her. She still has a conflict of interest, because the term names a risky situation, not proven bias.
questions.f: A consultant recommends a software platform and is paid a referral fee by its vendor, though nothing suggests the fee swayed her. She has no conflict of interest, because the term applies only once bias has been shown.
questions.x: On Thompson's definition a conflict is a condition, not conduct: it exists whenever circumstances create a substantial risk of undue influence. Proven bias would be a separate, more serious problem; the conflict is a reason to check, not a verdict.

questions.t: When an adviser discloses a conflict of interest, don't assume the disclosure makes her advice safe to use, since people tend to discount disclosed advice too little.
questions.f: When an adviser discloses a conflict of interest, you can assume the disclosure makes her advice safe to use, since people tend to discount disclosed advice more than enough.
questions.x: In the coin-jar experiments, advisees adjusted for disclosed conflicts only partly, partly because they anchored on the number given, while advisers inflated their advice further. Disclosure is information to act on, not a fix.

questions.t: A 2017 Cochrane review found that industry-sponsored drug and device studies kept their excess of favourable results even among papers rated at low risk of bias.
questions.f: A 2017 Cochrane review found that industry-sponsored drug and device studies lost their excess of favourable results once only papers rated at low risk of bias were counted.
questions.x: Standard quality checklists such as randomisation and allocation concealment did not account for the sponsorship effect. So a study passing those checks does not settle whether its funding shaped the result.

questions.t: "Every project in the portfolio has someone in finance who can sign off its budget, so someone in finance can sign off every project's budget." This inference commits the quantifier shift fallacy.
questions.f: "Every project in the portfolio has someone in finance who can sign off its budget, so someone in finance can sign off every project's budget." This inference is valid, since the premise already covers every project.
questions.x: The premise lets the approver differ from project to project; the conclusion demands one person for all of them. If sign-off rights are split by business unit, the premise is true and the conclusion false, so the form is invalid.

questions.t: To expose a quantifier shift, describe a case where each A gets its own B, so the premise holds while no single B serves every A.
questions.f: To expose a quantifier shift, describe a case where one single B serves every A, so the premise holds while the conclusion fails.
questions.x: A counterexample needs a true premise with a false conclusion. If one B serves every A, the conclusion is true, so nothing is shown; giving each A a different B, like a different teacher for each class, is what breaks the inference.

questions.t: Inferring "every x is related to some y" from "some single y is related to every x" is valid; only the step in the other direction is the quantifier shift fallacy.
questions.f: Inferring "some single y is related to every x" from "every x is related to some y" is valid; only the step in the other direction is the quantifier shift fallacy.
questions.x: "Someone loves everyone" guarantees that everyone is loved by someone, but not the reverse. Because one direction is valid and its mirror image is not, the slip is easy to make; check which quantifier comes first in each sentence.

questions.t: The office thermostat reads 21 degrees, so a manager concludes the room is about 21 degrees. Facilities then reports that this thermostat's sensor has been faulty all week. That report is an undercutting defeater.
questions.f: The office thermostat reads 21 degrees, so a manager concludes the room is about 21 degrees. Facilities then reports that this thermostat's sensor has been faulty all week. That report is a rebutting defeater.
questions.x: The report gives no reason to think the room isn't 21 degrees; it only shows the reading can't support that conclusion here, which is undercutting. A rebutting defeater would be direct evidence of a different temperature, such as a calibrated thermometer reading 26.

questions.t: When two equally strong default rules point to opposite conclusions about the same case, the reasonable response is to suspend judgment until something tips the balance.
questions.f: When two equally strong default rules point to opposite conclusions about the same case, the reasonable response is to go with whichever rule you applied first.
questions.x: In the classic case of someone who is both a Quaker (usually pacifist) and a Republican (usually not), each default defeats the other. Order of consideration is no reason to prefer one, so neither conclusion is justified yet.

questions.t: The idea of defeasibility entered modern philosophy from law, through H. L. A. Hart's 1949 argument that a claim like "there is a valid contract" can be defeated by a recognised exception.
questions.f: The idea of defeasibility entered modern philosophy from law, through John Pollock's 1949 argument that a claim like "there is a valid contract" can be defeated by a recognised exception.
questions.x: Hart, a legal philosopher, introduced the notion by noting that legal claims hold unless an exception applies. Pollock came decades later, building the theory of prima facie reasons and defeaters in 1987.

questions.t: A buyer's habit of choosing the best-known supplier served well for years, then starts failing after a wave of heavily advertised newcomers. Ecological rationality says to check first whether the environment changed.
questions.f: A buyer's habit of choosing the best-known supplier served well for years, then starts failing after a wave of heavily advertised newcomers. Ecological rationality says the failure shows the habit was irrational all along.
questions.x: A heuristic is smart only where its cue tracks the outcome; recognition worked while fame went with quality. Heavy advertising breaks that link, so the right diagnosis is a changed environment, and the remedy is to re-check the fit rather than condemn rules of thumb wholesale.

questions.t: Before trusting a rule of thumb for forecasts, test it on new cases rather than judging it by how well it fits the past cases it was built from.
questions.f: Before trusting a rule of thumb for forecasts, judge it by how well it fits the past cases it was built from rather than spending effort testing it on new cases.
questions.x: Flexible models can fit past data closely yet predict new cases badly, which is overfitting; simple rules often win on prediction precisely because they don't chase noise. Only out-of-sample performance shows whether a rule fits its environment.

questions.t: Hilbig and Richter's reanalysis of recognition data found that most individual participants did not behave like consistent one-reason heuristic users.
questions.f: Hilbig and Richter's reanalysis of recognition data found that nearly every individual participant relied on recognition alone, as consistent one-reason heuristic users would.
questions.x: Separating recognition use from use of other knowledge lowered estimated reliance on recognition, and few people looked like pure one-reason users. That is why the descriptive side of ecological rationality is contested even though the fit argument is well supported.

questions.t: Three trade-show visitors and two support tickets ask for a dark mode, and a product manager concludes most customers want it and makes it next quarter's top priority. That is a hasty generalization.
questions.f: Three trade-show visitors and two support tickets ask for a dark mode, and a product manager concludes most customers want it and makes it next quarter's top priority. That is the fallacy of accident.
questions.x: The manager leaps from five self-selected requests to a claim about the whole customer base, which is hasty generalization. The fallacy of accident runs the other way, misapplying a general rule to an unusual case.

questions.t: Whether a quick generalization from a few cases is fallacious depends partly on the stakes: a hunch that's fine for choosing a lunch spot can be reckless for a safety decision.
questions.f: Whether a quick generalization from a few cases is fallacious depends only on the sample, so a hunch from a few cases is just as faulty for choosing a lunch spot as for a safety decision.
questions.x: Walton and Gordon tie the fallacy to the standard of proof the setting demands. Low-stakes choices can run on thin evidence; when being wrong is costly, the same thin evidence is not enough, so raise the bar before acting.

questions.t: A 2020 meta-analysis found that anecdotes outpersuade statistics when people are emotionally engaged, as with severe threats, while statistics win when engagement is low.
questions.f: A 2020 meta-analysis found that statistics outpersuade anecdotes when people are emotionally engaged, as with severe threats, while anecdotes win when engagement is low.
questions.x: High emotional engagement tilts people toward vivid single stories, which helps explain how one memorable case turns into a general rule. That makes high-stakes, emotional topics exactly where to check for a proper sample.

questions.t: Six of eight hires on a new onboarding checklist got up to speed faster than average, so a manager budgets a company-wide rollout expecting the same 75% success rate. That expectation reflects belief in the law of small numbers.
questions.f: Six of eight hires on a new onboarding checklist got up to speed faster than average, so a manager budgets a company-wide rollout expecting the same 75% success rate. That expectation reflects the gambler's fallacy.
questions.x: The manager treats a tiny pilot as a faithful miniature of the whole population and expects its result to replicate, the core of the law of small numbers. The gambler's fallacy would be expecting the next outcomes to swing the other way to balance a streak.

questions.t: Before ranking fund managers on two strong years, ask how much spread pure chance would produce across all of them, since short records exaggerate differences in skill.
questions.f: Before ranking fund managers on two strong years, there's little need to ask how much spread chance would produce, since even short records mostly reflect real differences in skill.
questions.x: Rabin's model shows that believers in small samples see far more real variation in ability than exists, which he called fictitious variation. Comparing the observed spread with what luck alone would give is the check.

questions.t: Benjamin's 2018 review judged the gambler's fallacy well supported but the evidence for over-inference from small samples weak, noting that people more often under-infer in experiments.
questions.f: Benjamin's 2018 review judged over-inference from small samples well supported but the evidence for the gambler's fallacy weak, noting that people more often over-infer in experiments.
questions.x: The expectation that short runs balance out holds up across surveys, experiments and field data, but the broader claim that people jump to conclusions from small samples does not. That split is why the bias is rated contested.

questions.t: Told that 96% of a supplier's parts pass inspection, a reviewer restates it as 40 defects per 1,000 and checks that against the contract threshold. That habit makes her less open to being swayed by the positive framing.
questions.f: Told that 96% of a supplier's parts pass inspection, a reviewer restates it as 40 defects per 1,000 and checks that against the contract threshold. That habit makes her more open to being swayed by the positive framing.
questions.x: Converting a figure into another form and tying it to a decision threshold is what numerate people tend to do, and it lets the quantity rather than the wording drive the judgment. Less numerate readers rate the same supplier better when told "96% pass" than "4% fail".

questions.t: When presenting risk figures to a mixed audience, cut nonessential numbers and make higher numbers stand for better outcomes, which helps less numerate readers.
questions.f: When presenting risk figures to a mixed audience, include every available number so nothing is hidden, which helps less numerate readers most.
questions.x: Studies of risk communication found that low-numerate readers did better when figures were trimmed to what matters, ordered by relevance and aligned so bigger means better. Extra numbers add load without adding understanding for them.

questions.t: In a 2020 study of the affect heuristic, numeracy's link with weaker risk-benefit coupling vanished after controlling for abstract reasoning, while cognitive reflection remained a predictor.
questions.f: In a 2020 study of the affect heuristic, cognitive reflection's link with weaker risk-benefit coupling vanished after controlling for abstract reasoning, while numeracy remained a predictor.
questions.x: The result suggests numeracy may be standing in for general reasoning ability rather than causing the effect itself. Along with mostly correlational evidence, that is why claims that numeracy debiases are rated mixed.

questions.t: Tired of arguing case by case over which client dinners are "reasonable", a firm announces a fixed cap of $60 per person. It has replaced a standard with a bright-line rule.
questions.f: Tired of arguing case by case over which client dinners are "reasonable", a firm announces a fixed cap of $60 per person. It has replaced a bright-line rule with a standard.
questions.x: "Reasonable" is an open standard that gets its content only when someone judges each claim; a dollar cap fixed in advance is a sharp, easily checked criterion. The false version reverses which one the firm started with.

questions.t: Before adopting a sharp cutoff, ask which cases it will catch that its purpose would spare and which it will miss, since bright lines are both over- and under-inclusive.
questions.f: Before adopting a sharp cutoff, there's no need to ask which cases it will wrongly catch or miss, since a bright line, unlike a standard, fits its purpose in every case.
questions.x: The price of a clear rule is rigidity: an age, amount or date will sometimes hit cases it wasn't meant for and spare ones it was. Weighing that cost, and perhaps adding a narrow escape hatch, is part of drawing the line well.

questions.t: In Kaplow's economic analysis, rules cost more to write but less to apply, while standards are cheap to write but costly to interpret and adjudicate case by case.
questions.f: In Kaplow's economic analysis, standards cost more to write but less to apply, while rules are cheap to write but costly to interpret and adjudicate case by case.
questions.x: Kaplow framed the choice as a matter of timing: a rule front-loads the work of deciding, so each later case is quick to settle, while a standard defers that work to each case. Frequent, similar cases therefore favour rules.

questions.t: Since nobody can say exactly how many late deliveries make a supplier "unreliable", a buyer concludes there's no real difference between a supplier late twice a year and one late every week. That is the line-drawing fallacy.
questions.f: Since nobody can say exactly how many late deliveries make a supplier "unreliable", a buyer concludes there's no real difference between a supplier late twice a year and one late every week. That is a slippery slope.
questions.x: The buyer treats the lack of a sharp boundary as proof that the clear cases don't differ, which is the line-drawing fallacy; borderline cases don't erase clear ones. A slippery slope would instead warn that a first step leads to a feared outcome.

questions.t: To stop readers misreading "likely" in a risk report, put the numeric range in brackets right after the word, since tables or tooltips that readers must open help little.
questions.f: To stop readers misreading "likely" in a risk report, put the numeric ranges in a separate table or tooltip, which works better than brackets in the text.
questions.x: In a 2019 experiment, in-text brackets roughly doubled agreement with the official ranges, while tables and tooltips helped little because many readers never looked at them. A convention only cuts vagueness if readers actually see it.

questions.t: "Prime number" is general but not vague: it covers many different numbers, yet there are no borderline cases where it is unclear whether it applies.
questions.f: "Prime number" is vague but not general: it covers only a narrow set of numbers, yet there are borderline cases where it is unclear whether it applies.
questions.x: Vagueness means having borderline cases, not covering a wide range. Words like "bald" or "urgent" are vague; "prime number" applies to infinitely many numbers but always with a definite yes or no.

questions.t: Pressed to admit that shadowing gives more real practice than his onboarding course, a manager replies that "best training" can mean quickest to finish, not most practice. In the Topics' terms he is defending by distinguishing senses of a word.
questions.f: Pressed to admit that shadowing gives more real practice than his onboarding course, a manager replies that "best training" can mean quickest to finish, not most practice. In the Topics' terms he is defending by finding likenesses.
questions.x: He blocks the refutation by showing that "best" is used in two senses, one of Aristotle's four means of getting arguments. Finding likenesses would mean pointing to similarities between cases, which is not what his reply does.

questions.t: Refuting a colleague's thesis from premises she herself conceded shows her position is inconsistent, but on the Topics' account it does not by itself prove the opposite thesis true.
questions.f: Refuting a colleague's thesis from premises she herself conceded shows her position is inconsistent, and on the Topics' account it thereby proves the opposite thesis true.
questions.x: Dialectic works from what the other side grants, so it shows what follows from their concessions, not what is true. Before treating a won debate as a settled fact, check whether the conceded premises are themselves true.

questions.t: Book I of the Topics sorts every predication into four predicables: definition, property, genus and accident.
questions.f: Book I of the Topics sorts every predication into five predicables: definition, property, genus, species and accident.
questions.x: Aristotle's own list has four. Porphyry and later commentators expanded it to five, which is why the five-item version is familiar but not what the Topics says.

questions.t: "No contractors have badge access. Some visitors are contractors. So some visitors lack badge access." The premises plus the denied conclusion, "all visitors have badge access", form an inconsistent triad, so the syllogism is valid.
questions.f: "No contractors have badge access. Some visitors are contractors. So some visitors lack badge access." The premises plus the denied conclusion, "all visitors have badge access", can all be true together, so the syllogism is invalid.
questions.x: If all visitors had access, the visitors who are contractors would have access, contradicting "no contractors have access". The trio can't all be true, which is exactly what makes the original argument valid on Ladd's test.

questions.t: If your context assumes the classes involved have members, add that as an explicit premise before using the antilogism test, since the test reads universals as making no such claim.
questions.f: If your context assumes the classes involved have members, there's no need to add it as a premise before using the antilogism test, since the test already reads universals as claiming their classes have members.
questions.x: The test treats "all S are P" only as saying a combination is empty, so moods that rely on existential import come out invalid. Stating the existence assumption openly lets those arguments be judged fairly.

questions.t: Christine Ladd introduced the antilogism in 1883 as a graduate student of Charles S. Peirce at Johns Hopkins, which withheld her doctorate until 1926.
questions.f: Christine Ladd introduced the antilogism in 1883 as a graduate student of George Boole at Johns Hopkins, which withheld her doctorate until 1926.
questions.x: Ladd published the method in "On the Algebra of Logic" while studying under Peirce, who shaped her algebraic approach. Boole was an earlier founder of the algebra of logic, not her teacher.

questions.t: Asked whether last quarter's sales report is accurate, a director insists it must be, since admitting errors would rattle investors. Used to settle a question of fact, that is the fallacy of appeal to consequences.
questions.f: Asked whether last quarter's sales report is accurate, a director insists it must be, since admitting errors would rattle investors. Used to settle a question of fact, that is a reasonable argument from consequences.
questions.x: Consequences can be good reasons for deciding what to do, but they have no bearing on whether a report is true. The tell is the shift from "is it accurate?" to "what would be convenient?"

questions.t: Faced with an argument against a holiday-weekend system cutover because it risks an outage, also ask what waiting would cost, such as a support contract that lapses.
questions.f: Faced with an argument against a holiday-weekend system cutover because it risks an outage, the only fair question is how bad the outage would be, since what waiting would cost is beside the point.
questions.x: One of the critical questions for this scheme is whether there are consequences of the opposite value, such as costs of not acting. Weighing only the feared outcome makes a presumptive reason look like a decisive one.

questions.t: An argument from negative consequences becomes an argument from threat when the speaker is committed to bringing about the bad outcome; a mere warning lacks that commitment.
questions.f: An argument from negative consequences becomes an argument from threat when the bad outcome is severe, whoever would bring it about; a mere warning concerns only mild outcomes.
questions.x: What turns a warning into a threat is who causes the harm, not how big it is. Warning that heavy drinking risks early death is prudential; a professor promising a bad grade for defending a view is a threat.

questions.t: A stalled software rollout will cost more to finish than it can return, yet the IT director argues for more funding because $2 million has already gone into it. That is the sunk cost fallacy.
questions.f: A stalled software rollout will cost more to finish than it can return, yet the IT director argues for more funding because $2 million has already gone into it. That is the framing effect.
questions.x: The money already spent is gone whichever way the decision goes, so only remaining costs and benefits should count. Letting the past outlay drive further investment is the sunk cost fallacy; a framing effect would hinge on how the same options are worded.

questions.t: In Arkes and Blumer's 1985 studies, students who had taken economics showed the sunk cost effect about as much as those who had not.
questions.f: In Arkes and Blumer's 1985 studies, students who had taken economics showed a much weaker sunk cost effect than those who had not.
questions.x: Knowing the textbook rule that sunk costs are irrelevant did not protect people, and a later meta-analysis likewise found no benefit from economic familiarity. That is why changing how the decision is posed works better than simply teaching the rule.

questions.t: An analyst believes orders over $500 need a manager's sign-off, then spots a routine $620 order without one. Rather than report a breach, she checks whether the threshold changed. Doubting the rule here can be reasonable.
questions.f: An analyst believes orders over $500 need a manager's sign-off, then spots a routine $620 order without one. Rather than report a breach, she checks whether the threshold changed. Doubting the rule here is unreasonable, since her beliefs imply a breach.
questions.x: On Harman's view, logic says what her beliefs imply but not whether to accept the conclusion or drop a premise. Which move is right depends on how confident she is in each belief, and a routine unsigned order is a fair reason to doubt the rule.

questions.t: When a team argues over whether to ship on Friday, settle the factual questions apart from the decision itself, since deciding what to do also needs goals and values the facts don't supply.
questions.f: When a team argues over whether to ship on Friday, there's no need to keep the factual questions apart from the decision, since once the facts are settled the right action follows from them alone.
questions.x: Theoretical reasoning settles what to believe; practical reasoning settles what to do and draws on goals as well as facts. Keeping the two apart shows whether a disagreement is about the evidence or about priorities.

questions.t: In a 2014 study by Trouche, Sander and Mercier, 22% of adults solved a disjunctive logic problem alone, but 63% did after group discussion.
questions.f: In a 2014 study by Trouche, Sander and Mercier, 63% of adults solved a disjunctive logic problem alone, but only 22% did after group discussion.
questions.x: Groups did far better, mostly because good arguments rather than confidence changed minds, as the argumentative theory of reasoning predicts. The authors also found a problem where confident wrong members prevailed, so discussion helps but guarantees nothing.

questions.t: When planning a study's sample size, base the effect size on the smallest effect worth detecting rather than on one estimated from a small pilot, since a pilot's estimate is too imprecise.
questions.f: When planning a study's sample size, base the effect size on the one estimated from a small pilot rather than on the smallest effect worth detecting, since the pilot measured it directly.
questions.x: Small pilots give noisy effect estimates, and published effects are inflated by publication bias, so plans built on them overstate power. Anchoring on the smallest effect that would matter in practice is the strongest justification.

questions.t: Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer found that by 1984, median power to detect a medium effect in the journal Cohen had reviewed had fallen from .46 to .37.
questions.f: Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer found that by 1984, median power to detect a medium effect in the journal Cohen had reviewed had risen from .37 to .46.
questions.x: Decades after Cohen warned that studies were underpowered, power had got worse, and almost no experiments even mentioned it. Advice alone did not change practice, which is why sample-size planning is now pushed through journals and preregistration.

questions.t: Rushing through a vendor pitch the night before a budget deadline, a team lead approves it mainly because the deck shows a famous client's logo, without reading the pricing terms. In ELM terms she was persuaded by the peripheral route.
questions.f: Rushing through a vendor pitch the night before a budget deadline, a team lead approves it mainly because the deck shows a famous client's logo, without reading the pricing terms. In ELM terms she was persuaded by the central route.
questions.x: The central route means weighing the merits of the arguments, which she skipped; a familiar logo is a simple cue, and time pressure lowered her ability to think it through. A useful check is whether you could restate the pitch's best argument or only name its messenger.

questions.t: To counter the sunk cost fallacy, pose the decision as a fresh choice and judge whether you would start the project today for what it will still cost.
questions.f: To counter the sunk cost fallacy, tally everything already spent on the project so the full past investment is in view before deciding whether to continue.
questions.x: Putting past spending front and centre feeds the bias rather than checking it. The fresh-start framing strips the sunk cost out and leaves only the future costs and benefits that should decide.

questions.t: An HR team pilots a new onboarding programme on one quarter's 15 hires, though a power calculation said it needed about four quarters per group. A non-significant pilot result would be uninformative about whether the programme works.
questions.f: An HR team pilots a new onboarding programme on one quarter's 15 hires, though a power calculation said it needed about four quarters per group. A non-significant pilot result would be good evidence that the programme fails.
questions.x: An underpowered study has a high chance of missing a real effect, so a null result from it says little, and a positive one would be fragile. The honest options are to gather more data, narrow the question, or label the pilot exploratory.

questions.t: Pat trusts the new supplier but distrusts the firm that sent last month's late shipment, and concludes they must be two different companies. Inferring non-identity from a difference in attitudes is the masked-man fallacy.
questions.f: Pat trusts the new supplier but distrusts the firm that sent last month's late shipment, and concludes they must be two different companies. Inferring non-identity from a difference in attitudes is the quantifier shift fallacy.
questions.x: The tell is using what someone trusts or knows to prove two things are distinct; the firms could be one company under another name. A quantifier shift swaps the order of 'every' and 'some', which nothing here does.

questions.t: Before accepting that a colleague 'believes the head of office was unfair' because they think the anonymous reviewer was unfair, ask whether the colleague knows the reviewer and the head are the same person.
questions.f: Before accepting that a colleague 'believes the head of office was unfair' because they think the anonymous reviewer was unfair, ask whether the reviewer and the head are in fact the same person.
questions.x: The identity can be perfectly true and the substituted belief report still false, because belief depends on how the person thinks of the individual. So the key check is whether the believer knows the identity, not merely whether it holds.

questions.t: The masked-man fallacy takes its name from a veiled-man puzzle credited to Eubulides of the Megarian school in the fourth century BCE.
questions.f: The masked-man fallacy takes its name from a veiled-man puzzle credited to Gottlob Frege in his 1892 work on sense and reference.
questions.x: The puzzle of knowing your father but not the masked man who is your father is attributed to Eubulides, alongside the liar and the heap. Frege came much later and supplied a diagnosis, sense versus reference, not the puzzle itself.

questions.t: A hiring panel asked how well a candidate will perform over three years ends up scoring how impressive the interview presentation was, and feels it answered the question. That is attribute substitution.
questions.f: A hiring panel asked how well a candidate will perform over three years ends up scoring how impressive the interview presentation was, and feels it answered the question. That is the availability heuristic.
questions.x: A hard target (future performance) was quietly replaced by an easier, accessible attribute (presentation polish). Availability is the narrower case where ease of recall stands in for frequency, and nobody here is recalling examples.

questions.t: To help a team catch an attribute substitution, make the neglected factor, such as the base rate, explicit and salient; time pressure and a good mood make an unchecked swap more likely.
questions.f: To help a team catch an attribute substitution, make the neglected factor, such as the base rate, explicit and salient; time pressure and a good mood make an unchecked swap less likely.
questions.x: Deliberate checking of intuitive answers is light, so it helps to put the ignored quantity in plain view. Time pressure, concurrent load and good mood weaken that checking rather than strengthen it.

questions.t: Shah and Oppenheimer's 2008 review called attribute substitution a partial account of heuristics, since it misses other effort savings such as examining fewer alternatives.
questions.f: Shah and Oppenheimer's 2008 review called attribute substitution a partial account of heuristics, since it misses other effort savings such as relying on easy-to-access cues.
questions.x: Reliance on accessible cues is exactly what substitution does explain; the gap the review pointed to was other shortcuts, like considering fewer options or simplifying cue weights. That critique is why the model's status is mixed.

questions.t: A policy requires receipts "for meals and taxi fares over $25", and an employee concludes an $18 client lunch needs none, though finance meant every meal. Relying on the other way of grouping the phrase is amphiboly.
questions.f: A policy requires receipts "for meals and taxi fares over $25", and an employee concludes an $18 client lunch needs none, though finance meant every meal. Relying on the other way of grouping the phrase is equivocation.
questions.x: Every word keeps its meaning; what shifts is whether "over $25" attaches to meals as well as taxis, a structural ambiguity. Equivocation needs a single word that changes meaning between premise and conclusion.

questions.t: To keep a rule from being read two ways, repeat the qualifier for each item, as in "meals of any amount; taxi fares over $25", and split long lists so only one grammatical structure is possible.
questions.f: To keep a rule from being read two ways, state the qualifier once at the end, as in "meals and taxi fares over $25", and merge items into one list so only one grammatical structure is possible.
questions.x: Amphiboly feeds on lists and modifiers that can attach in more than one place. Repeating the qualifier and splitting the list removes the second parse, whereas one trailing qualifier over a merged list is exactly what creates it.

questions.t: William of Ockham's Summa Logicae defined amphiboly as a whole sentence with several senses although none of its individual terms is ambiguous.
questions.f: William of Ockham's Summa Logicae defined amphiboly as a single term with several senses although the sentence's grammatical structure is unambiguous.
questions.x: Ockham located amphiboly in the structure of the whole sentence, giving rules for constructions that produce it. A single term with several senses is the mark of equivocation, the contrasting fallacy.

questions.t: A device match is 200 times more probable if a given employee filed a disputed claim than if someone else did, and an analyst concludes the employee very likely filed it, though thousands of staff could have. The reasoning skips the prior odds.
questions.f: A device match is 200 times more probable if a given employee filed a disputed claim than if someone else did, and an analyst concludes the employee very likely filed it, though thousands of staff could have. The reasoning is sound.
questions.x: A likelihood ratio measures only how strongly the finding favours one proposition; it must be multiplied by the prior odds. With thousands of possible submitters and nothing else pointing to this person, the posterior can still favour innocence.

questions.t: Before multiplying the likelihood ratios of two pieces of evidence, check they are independent: two cameras recording the same person are not, and multiplying their ratios overstates the joint strength.
questions.f: Before multiplying the likelihood ratios of two pieces of evidence, check they are independent: two cameras recording the same person are not, and multiplying their ratios understates the joint strength.
questions.x: Multiplying assumes each item adds fresh information. Two dependent items largely repeat each other, so treating them as independent counts the same support twice and inflates it.

questions.t: In Thompson and Newman's 2015 experiment, 86% of those given a likelihood ratio misread it as the chance the defendant was the source, against 26% of those given a verbal statement.
questions.f: In Thompson and Newman's 2015 experiment, 26% of those given a likelihood ratio misread it as the chance the defendant was the source, against 86% of those given a verbal statement.
questions.x: The numeric likelihood ratio drew the most transposed readings, more even than random match probabilities at 78%, while verbal statements drew far fewer. The framework disciplines experts but does not by itself fix how listeners hear it.

questions.t: Asked what an economist would advise about a non-refundable workshop that has turned out useless, a trainee says, "Waste not, want not: attend, or the fee is wasted." That is a common lay theory, not the economist's rule.
questions.f: Asked what an economist would advise about a non-refundable workshop that has turned out useless, a trainee says, "Waste not, want not: attend, or the fee is wasted." That is the sunk cost principle economists endorse.
questions.x: The fee is gone whichever way the trainee chooses, so the sunk cost principle says to ignore it and judge the day on its remaining value. Untrained students mostly believed economists would back "waste not, want not", and correcting that belief is part of the training.

questions.t: When training staff to ignore sunk costs, mix in cases where continuing is the right call, so they don't come away with a blanket "always quit" rule.
questions.f: When training staff to ignore sunk costs, use only cases where quitting is the right call, so they don't come away with a blanket "always quit" rule.
questions.x: Pairing sunk cost problems with extra cost problems, where continuing is correct, forces learners to weigh what each option still costs and returns. A diet of quit-only examples teaches exactly the blanket rule it aims to avoid.

questions.t: In Larrick, Morgan and Nisbett's 1990 training study, students taught the sunk cost rule only with money examples applied it fully to problems about time and effort too.
questions.f: In Larrick, Morgan and Nisbett's 1990 training study, students taught the sunk cost rule only with money examples applied it to money problems but not to problems about time and effort.
questions.x: Both the financial-only and the non-financial-only training groups beat controls on every kind of problem, showing domain-general transfer. That transfer is what makes abstract rule training promising, unlike generic economics coursework.

questions.t: A planner argues that switching the retirement plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment, with the same terms, can't change much, since anyone who values the plan will join anyway. Automatic-enrollment field evidence shows this reasoning fails.
questions.f: A planner argues that switching the retirement plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment, with the same terms, can't change much, since anyone who values the plan will join anyway. Automatic-enrollment field evidence shows this reasoning holds.
questions.x: When a large employer made enrollment automatic without changing terms, participation rose substantially and new hires tended to keep the defaults, which the authors put down to inertia and reading the default as advice. The planner's model assumes attention and willpower people don't reliably have.

questions.t: A 2016 project replicating 18 laboratory experiments from two top economics journals found a significant effect in the original direction for 11 of them, about 61%.
questions.f: A 2016 project replicating 18 laboratory experiments from two top economics journals found a significant effect in the original direction for 7 of them, about 39%.
questions.x: Eleven of 18 replicated, with effects averaging about two-thirds of the originals' size, so the field's lab base held up better than many psychology findings. Smaller replicated effects are still a reminder that originals tend to be inflated.

questions.t: Maier and colleagues argued in 2022 that once publication bias is corrected for, the evidence for nudges in general is not convincing, though some individual nudges may still work.
questions.f: Maier and colleagues argued in 2022 that once publication bias is corrected for, the evidence for nudges in general grows stronger, though some individual nudges may still fail.
questions.x: Correcting for publication bias removes the inflation from unpublished null results, and here it left the general case for nudging unconvincing. The policy branch of the field is therefore more disputed than its laboratory findings.

questions.t: When a video call that looks and sounds like a senior manager asks for an urgent payment, the robust check is to call the manager back on a known number, not to study the video for glitches.
questions.f: When a video call that looks and sounds like a senior manager asks for an urgent payment, the robust check is to study the video for glitches, not to call the manager back on a known number.
questions.x: People are poor at spotting deepfake artefacts, so inspecting the media is unreliable. Verifying the instruction through an independent channel works however convincing the fake is, because it checks provenance rather than appearance.

questions.t: A manager caught on a genuine recording promising a client a refund later waves it away as "probably a deepfake". Using public awareness of deepfakes to deny real evidence is the liar's dividend.
questions.f: A manager caught on a genuine recording promising a client a refund later waves it away as "probably a deepfake". Using public awareness of deepfakes to deny real evidence is the overconfidence effect.
questions.x: The tell is a real recording being dismissed by pointing to the possibility of fakes, the reverse risk deepfakes create. The overconfidence effect is about viewers trusting their own detection skill more than their accuracy warrants.

questions.t: In Köbis and colleagues' 2021 experiment, people sorted short videos into real and deepfake correctly only 57.6% of the time, and neither an awareness prompt nor a cash incentive improved that.
questions.f: In Köbis and colleagues' 2021 experiment, people sorted short videos into real and deepfake correctly only 57.6% of the time, but a cash incentive raised that to about 75%.
questions.x: Accuracy was barely above chance and stayed there under both an awareness prompt and a financial incentive, while participants overrated their own skill. Trying harder to look closely is not a reliable defence.

questions.t: A project lead approves each change request because one extra day can't turn an on-schedule project into a late one, until thirty requests later it is plainly late. Each step leans on tolerance, the engine of a sorites.
questions.f: A project lead approves each change request because one extra day can't turn an on-schedule project into a late one, until thirty requests later it is plainly late. Each step leans on a predicted chain of consequences, the engine of a slippery slope.
questions.x: The lead's premise is that a vague predicate like "on schedule" survives any change too small to matter, which is tolerance; repeated, those harmless steps accumulate. A slippery slope instead warns that one step will cause the next, which nobody claims here.

questions.t: The line-drawing version of the sorites runs in reverse: since one grain is not a heap and a million grains are, there must be an exact number of grains at which heaps begin.
questions.f: The mathematical-induction version of the sorites runs in reverse: since one grain is not a heap and a million grains are, there must be an exact number of grains at which heaps begin.
questions.x: The line-drawing version uses the least-number principle to force a sharp boundary, which seems just as incredible. The induction version instead packs all the small steps into one premise: for every n, if n grains aren't a heap, n+1 aren't either.

questions.t: In forced-march colour-categorisation tasks, Egré, de Gardelle and Ripley found people switched labels earlier than expected, the opposite of the hysteresis contextualist accounts predicted.
questions.f: In forced-march colour-categorisation tasks, Egré, de Gardelle and Ripley found people kept the starting label longer than expected, the hysteresis contextualist accounts predicted.
questions.x: Contextualists expected people to cling to the first label during a forced march, but participants switched early, an effect the authors called enhanced contrast. Such small, task-specific results inform the debate without settling it.

questions.t: In the preface to his Treatise on Light, Huygens held that a theory is best supported when it foresees new phenomena that are later confirmed, more than when it merely fits facts already known.
questions.f: In the preface to his Treatise on Light, Huygens held that a theory is best supported when it fits many facts already known, more than when it foresees new phenomena that are later confirmed.
questions.x: Huygens gave novel predictions extra weight, alongside the idea that many matching consequences raise a theory's probability. Fitting known facts is easier, since a theory can be shaped around them.

questions.t: Testing a hypothesis Huygens's way, if a predicted consequence fails you still have to ask which of the theory's assumptions is at fault, a question his account leaves open.
questions.f: Testing a hypothesis Huygens's way, if a predicted consequence fails you can blame the main hypothesis itself, a question his account settles.
questions.x: Jeffrey noted that Huygens showed how agreement raises probability but not how much, nor what to blame when a prediction fails. That gap is the holism problem the Duhem-Quine thesis presses.

questions.t: Huygens introduced mathematical expectation in his 1657 tract on games of chance, often called the first book on mathematical probability.
questions.f: Huygens introduced mathematical expectation in his 1690 Treatise on Light, often called the first book on mathematical probability.
questions.x: Expectation came from the short 1657 tract De ratiociniis in ludo aleae, later reprinted by Jakob Bernoulli. The Treatise on Light is the optics work whose preface states his method of testing hypotheses.

questions.t: An office manager reasons that the shared printer fails because of either the network or the print driver; diagnostics clear the network, so the driver is to blame. The inference is a valid disjunctive syllogism.
questions.f: An office manager reasons that the shared printer fails because of either the network or the print driver; diagnostics clear the network, so the driver is to blame. The inference affirms a disjunct.
questions.x: The manager denies one option and accepts the other, the valid elimination pattern. Affirming a disjunct runs the other way, confirming one option to rule the other out; any weakness here lies in whether the two-option list is complete.

questions.t: Disjunctive syllogism is valid whether "or" is read inclusively or exclusively, unlike the look-alike that confirms one option in order to reject the other.
questions.f: Disjunctive syllogism is valid only when "or" is read exclusively, like the look-alike that confirms one option in order to reject the other.
questions.x: On a truth table the only row where "P or Q" and "not P" are both true has Q true, under either reading of "or". The look-alike needs exclusivity, since with inclusive "or" both options can hold.

questions.t: Paraconsistent logics deny that disjunctive syllogism is valid in general, because it is a step in deriving the classical result that a contradiction implies every statement.
questions.f: Paraconsistent logics deny that modus ponens is valid in general, because it is a step in deriving the classical result that a contradiction implies every statement.
questions.x: From A you infer "A or B", and from "not A" disjunctive syllogism yields any B, so blocking explosion means giving up that step. Relevance logics in fact add a separate conditional precisely so that modus ponens survives.

questions.t: To learn how 4,000 field technicians rate a new scheduling app, a manager surveys whoever visits head office this month. That convenience sample risks a bias that surveying more visitors would not cure.
questions.f: To learn how 4,000 field technicians rate a new scheduling app, a manager surveys whoever visits head office this month. That convenience sample risks only sampling error, which surveying more visitors would cure.
questions.x: Technicians who come to head office may differ systematically from those who don't, which is sampling bias; size shrinks only the luck-of-the-draw error. Drawing names at random from the full staff list is what removes the bias.

questions.t: To learn whether a training course causes better performance, randomly assign who takes it; randomly sampling whom you study supports generalising to a population, not causal conclusions.
questions.f: To learn whether a training course causes better performance, randomly sample whom you study; randomly assigning who takes it supports generalising to a population, not causal conclusions.
questions.x: Random assignment spreads lurking variables evenly across treatment groups, which is what licenses a causal claim. Random sampling decides who is studied and lets you generalise from the sample to the population.

questions.t: A 2012 reanalysis of the failed 1936 Literary Digest poll traced its error mainly to non-response bias, finding that car and telephone owners actually favoured Roosevelt.
questions.f: A 2012 reanalysis of the failed 1936 Literary Digest poll traced its error mainly to its frame of car and telephone owners, finding that those owners heavily favoured Landon.
questions.x: The textbook story blames a frame of car and phone owners, but Gallup data showed those owners leaned to Roosevelt, so who chose to reply mattered more. Either way, millions of returns could not rescue a sample not selected, or answered, by chance.

questions.t: A manager once ruled a smartwatch breached a "no personal devices on the floor" policy because it could distract operators. An employee argues his screenless fitness band differs, since it can't distract. He is distinguishing the precedent.
questions.f: A manager once ruled a smartwatch breached a "no personal devices on the floor" policy because it could distract operators. An employee argues his screenless fitness band differs, since it can't distract. He is arguing by analogy from the precedent.
questions.x: Distinguishing points to a material factual difference (no screen) that takes the new case outside the earlier ruling's rationale. Arguing by analogy is the supervisor's move: stressing the similarity, that both are personal electronic devices.

questions.t: When a borderline case meets a rule, ask whether it sits in the rule's clear core or its penumbra, and if in the penumbra, whether the rule's purpose reaches it.
questions.f: When a borderline case meets a rule, ask whether it sits in the rule's clear core or its penumbra, and if in the penumbra, settle it by the rule's literal words alone.
questions.x: Hart's park example shows that the words settle core cases, like an ordinary car, but not penumbral ones, like a bicycle. There the words run out, so the useful question is why the rule exists and whether that reason applies.

questions.t: On Edward Levi's account of reasoning by example, legal rules change as they are used, because each new judgment of similarity between cases reshapes the rule.
questions.f: On Edward Levi's account of reasoning by example, legal rules stay fixed as they are used, because each new case is matched against the rule as first announced.
questions.x: Levi's three steps are seeing a similarity, announcing the rule implicit in the first case, and applying it to the second. Since the announced rule depends on which similarities are judged relevant, it shifts with each new case.

questions.t: An analyst role requires "experience" with the reporting database, and a recruiter marks a candidate as qualified because they once did a one-hour vendor tutorial on it. The recruiter's reasoning is an equivocation.
questions.f: An analyst role requires "experience" with the reporting database, and a recruiter marks a candidate as qualified because they once did a one-hour vendor tutorial on it. The recruiter's reasoning is an amphiboly.
questions.x: The single word "experience" shifts from sustained hands-on work in the requirement to any exposure at all in the note. Amphiboly would need a sentence whose grammar allows two parses, not one word with two senses.

questions.t: Van Laar argued that equivocation on related senses of one word misleads more than on unrelated senses like "bank", since a broad reading seems to cover both senses.
questions.f: Van Laar argued that equivocation on unrelated senses like "bank" misleads more than on related senses of one word, since a broad reading seems to cover both senses.
questions.x: Unrelated senses (homonymy) are easy to notice and rarely fool anyone. Related senses (polysemy) admit a vague umbrella reading, so the shift slips past even an attentive listener.

questions.t: Facing a suspected equivocation, a listener can answer with distinguo, simply stating which sense of the term they accept in each premise; the full charge of equivocation is the stronger move that must show how the argument misleads.
questions.f: Facing a suspected equivocation, a listener can answer with the full charge of equivocation, simply stating which sense of the term they accept in each premise; distinguo is the stronger move that must show how the argument misleads.
questions.x: Distinguo is the lighter reply: it separates the senses and lets the arguer pick one and defend the doubted premise. Alleging equivocation outright carries the burden of showing how the shift misleads.

questions.t: A team lead sizes each step of a reporting migration and promises three weeks, though the last two migrations took seven, because each had a "one-off" problem that won't recur. That is the planning fallacy.
questions.f: A team lead sizes each step of a reporting migration and promises three weeks, though the last two migrations took seven, because each had a "one-off" problem that won't recur. That is overprecision.
questions.x: The tell is knowing past jobs overran yet explaining the overruns away as special and forecasting from the plan's steps alone. Overprecision is about too-narrow confidence ranges; the lead gave no range at all.

questions.t: Planning backward from the deadline rather than forward from today led people in a 2016 study to predict later finishes, with no significant optimistic bias.
questions.f: Planning backward from the deadline rather than forward from today led people in a 2016 study to predict earlier finishes, with an even larger optimistic bias.
questions.x: Backward planners gave later, and on average unbiased, completion estimates, while forward planners again underestimated. The study left the mechanism unclear, so treat it as a useful tactic rather than a full explanation.

questions.t: Roy and Christenfeld (2007) argued that people underestimate how long future tasks will take partly because they misremember past tasks as having taken less time than they did.
questions.f: Roy and Christenfeld (2007) argued that people underestimate how long future tasks will take partly because they misremember past tasks as having taken more time than they did.
questions.x: If memory shrinks past durations, even a forecaster who consults the past starts from too-short figures. That challenges the idea that the error comes only from neglecting the past; checking recorded durations, not recollections, addresses it.

questions.t: "All incident-response team members are first-aid certified. All incident-response team members are full-time staff. So all full-time staff are first-aid certified." This syllogism commits the illicit minor.
questions.f: "All incident-response team members are first-aid certified. All incident-response team members are full-time staff. So all full-time staff are first-aid certified." This syllogism commits the illicit major.
questions.x: The conclusion's subject, "full-time staff", covers every employee there but only part of the class in the premise, where it is the predicate of an affirmative statement. An illicit major would overextend the conclusion's predicate instead.

questions.t: "All pilot-store managers use the new app; all pilot-store managers are regional staff; so all regional staff use it." If there are pilot managers, the most these premises support is that some regional staff use the app.
questions.f: "All pilot-store managers use the new app; all pilot-store managers are regional staff; so all regional staff use it." If there are pilot managers, the most these premises support is that most regional staff use the app.
questions.x: The evidence covers only the pilot managers, a part of the regional staff of unknown size, so only a "some" conclusion is earned. Offering that weaker claim is the repair; "most" still outruns what the premises say.

questions.t: Carveth Read noted that an illicit minor can survive scrutiny when its conclusion happens to be true, since a reader who agrees with it may not notice the invalid form.
questions.f: Carveth Read noted that an illicit minor can survive scrutiny when its conclusion happens to be false, since a reader who rejects it may not notice the invalid form.
questions.x: Read's example ends with the true claim that all cooking animals are men, which hides the flawed step. Validity depends on form, so a believable conclusion is no evidence the reasoning is sound.

questions.t: A manager can list every question to ask about a vendor's claim that its programme cut turnover by a third, yet skips them all because it's the result she hoped for. What she lacks is the disposition of critical thinking, not the ability.
questions.f: A manager can list every question to ask about a vendor's claim that its programme cut turnover by a third, yet skips them all because it's the result she hoped for. What she lacks is the ability of critical thinking, not the disposition.
questions.x: She has the skills, since she knows the checks; what fails is the habit of applying them, especially to a welcome result. Accounts of critical thinking treat abilities and dispositions as separate ingredients that can come apart.

questions.t: Because critical thinking leans heavily on domain knowledge and trained skills transfer weakly, Willingham advises planning critical-thinking instruction subject by subject over several years.
questions.f: Because critical thinking leans heavily on domain knowledge and trained skills transfer weakly, Willingham advises teaching it once as a general course that students then apply in every subject.
questions.x: If skills don't carry over well to new contexts, a single general course is exactly what would underdeliver. Building the skills inside each subject, where the needed knowledge lives, follows from his premises.

questions.t: Edward Glaser showed experimentally in 1941 that high-school students' critical thinking could be improved, after progressive schools of the 1930s had adopted it as a goal.
questions.f: John Dewey showed experimentally in 1941 that high-school students' critical thinking could be improved, after progressive schools of the 1930s had adopted it as a goal.
questions.x: Glaser's experiment was the early evidence that the skill can be taught. Dewey's contribution came earlier and was conceptual: his 1910 account of reflective thinking put the idea on the educational agenda.

questions.t: Choosing between two cloud vendors for a pilot, an officer has heard of only one, and only because of its widely reported outage. Picking it by name recognition is a poor bet here, since that familiarity isn't linked to reliability.
questions.f: Choosing between two cloud vendors for a pilot, an officer has heard of only one, and only because of its widely reported outage. Picking it by name recognition is a sound bet here, since any familiarity tracks reliability.
questions.x: The recognition heuristic works only when recognition correlates with the criterion. Familiarity that comes from a bad event is unrelated or even opposed to reliability, so the key question is why the name is familiar.

questions.t: If you already hold conclusive knowledge about the criterion, such as both vendors' audited uptime, use it rather than which name you recognise, since the recognition heuristic was never meant for that case.
questions.f: If you already hold conclusive knowledge about the criterion, such as both vendors' audited uptime, still go by which name you recognise, since the recognition heuristic was meant to override that knowledge.
questions.x: Recognition is a stand-in for missing knowledge, a cue for inference from memory when better information is absent. With conclusive facts in hand, the heuristic's own authors say it does not apply.

questions.t: In 2016 experiments with fictitious city names, 74% of choices followed recognition against 50% by chance, yet people still weighed other information they had.
questions.f: In 2016 experiments with fictitious city names, 74% of choices followed recognition against 50% by chance, and people ignored all other information once recognition discriminated.
questions.x: Basehore and Anderson found recognition a real basis for choice but not a strictly one-reason rule, arguing raw adherence rates overstate its sole influence. That is why the noncompensatory claim remains contested.

questions.t: A badge log shows a partial card ID that only 1 in 1,000 cards would share by chance, and security concludes there is a 99.9% chance the matching employee entered the server room. That is the prosecutor's fallacy.
questions.f: A badge log shows a partial card ID that only 1 in 1,000 cards would share by chance, and security concludes there is a 99.9% chance the matching employee entered the server room. That is the defense attorney's fallacy.
questions.x: The 1-in-1,000 figure is the chance of a match if the employee didn't enter, not the chance they didn't enter given the match; with 5,000 cards, about five others would match. The defense attorney's fallacy errs the other way, writing a match off as worthless.

questions.t: When correcting a prosecutor's fallacy, don't swing to treating a match as worthless because many people share the trait: narrowing a million possible sources to a few thousand is still strong evidence.
questions.f: When correcting a prosecutor's fallacy, it's right to treat a match as worthless because many people share the trait: narrowing a million possible sources to a few thousand leaves it weak evidence.
questions.x: Overcorrecting is the defense attorney's fallacy. A trait shared by thousands still cuts the field dramatically, so it should be combined with the rest of the case rather than discarded.

questions.t: In Thompson and Schumann's 1987 experiment, 22.2% committed the prosecutor's fallacy when a 2% hair-match rate was given as a conditional probability, against 4.2% when it also came as a count of people in a city.
questions.f: In Thompson and Schumann's 1987 experiment, 4.2% committed the prosecutor's fallacy when a 2% hair-match rate was given as a conditional probability, against 22.2% when it also came as a count of people in a city.
questions.x: Stating how many people in a city of a million would share the trait made the transposition far rarer. Restating rates as counts of people is a practical guard against the error.

questions.t: A $9,000 service contract covers a machine with a 10% chance of a $60,000 breakdown, an expected loss of $6,000. For a small firm where that hit would threaten payroll, buying the contract can still maximise expected utility.
questions.f: A $9,000 service contract covers a machine with a 10% chance of a $60,000 breakdown, an expected loss of $6,000. For a small firm where that hit would threaten payroll, expected utility theory says to skip it, since its price exceeds the expected loss.
questions.x: Expected utility weighs what outcomes are worth to this chooser, not their cash value, and a payroll-threatening loss costs far more than six times the pain of a $9,000 bill. Skipping it is what a pure expected-money calculation says, as with Bernoulli's insured merchant.

questions.t: If your preference between two risky options flips when you change an outcome they both share, you are violating the independence axiom and should ask which of your judgments to trust.
questions.f: If your preference between two risky options flips when you change an outcome they both share, you are violating the transitivity axiom and should ask which of your judgments to trust.
questions.x: Independence says that mixing options with a common outcome shouldn't reverse their ranking, which is what Allais-type flips break. Transitivity concerns chains of preference, such as preferring A to B and B to C but C to A.

questions.t: Starmer's 2000 review concluded that expected utility theory is likely to mislead as a description of choice in important contexts, though it fitted a substantial minority of individual subjects as well as any rival.
questions.f: Starmer's 2000 review concluded that expected utility theory is likely to mislead as a description of choice in important contexts, and that it fitted no individual subjects as well as its rivals did.
questions.x: Starmer recommended rank-dependent models such as cumulative prospect theory as the descriptive default, yet some individuals were still best described by expected utility. The theory's descriptive record is poor overall but not uniformly so.

questions.t: A team lead objects to making the weekly status meeting fortnightly, and also objects to making it twice weekly, but can't say why weekly is best beyond habit. By the reversal test, her original objection deserves less weight.
questions.f: A team lead objects to making the weekly status meeting fortnightly, and also objects to making it twice weekly, but can't say why weekly is best beyond habit. By the reversal test, her original objection deserves more weight.
questions.x: Rejecting change in both directions implies the current value is a rare optimum, which needs a reason. With only habit behind it, the double rejection points to status quo bias rather than confirming that weekly is ideal.

questions.t: If you reject a change in both directions, real transition costs of switching are a legitimate reason the current value may be best, and can meet the reversal test's burden.
questions.f: If you reject a change in both directions, the fact that it's how things have always been done is a legitimate reason the current value may be best, and can meet the reversal test's burden.
questions.x: Bostrom and Ord accept grounds such as transition costs, long adaptation to stable conditions, or risks of change. "We've always done it this way" is exactly the habit the test is built to expose, not a reason that answers it.

questions.t: Nebel argued in 2015 that preferring the status quo can be rational, because there is reason to preserve existing things of value even when replacements would be just as good.
questions.f: Nebel argued in 2015 that preferring the status quo is never rational, because there is no reason to preserve existing things of value when replacements would be just as good.
questions.x: On Nebel's view a person can reject change in both directions without being biased, which limits what the reversal test shows. He still treats the test as a fallible guide, part of why its status is contested.

questions.t: A vendor says its wellness app "cut sick days by 30%", citing a case study of one firm that adopted it. On the hierarchy of evidence that is a single uncontrolled case near the bottom, so a randomised pilot is a sensible next step.
questions.f: A vendor says its wellness app "cut sick days by 30%", citing a case study of one firm that adopted it. On the hierarchy of evidence real-world adoption ranks near the top, so the contract can be signed on that basis.
questions.x: One firm with no comparison group can't rule out other explanations, such as a mild flu season or other policy changes. Seeking a controlled comparison, or running a randomised pilot across departments, looks for the stronger evidence first.

questions.t: Treat a study design's rank as a starting point: an observational study with a very large effect or a clear dose-response gradient can be rated up, and a badly run trial rated down.
questions.f: Treat a study design's rank as fixed: an observational study with a very large effect or a clear dose-response gradient still sits below any trial, however badly the trial was run.
questions.x: Design is only a rough stand-in for risk of bias. Approaches like GRADE adjust certainty for features such as effect size, dose-response, inconsistency and imprecision, rather than reading quality off the design label.

questions.t: For a question about how common something is locally, the 2011 OCEBM Levels rank a current local survey first, whereas for a treatment's benefits a systematic review of randomised trials ranks first.
questions.f: For a question about how common something is locally, the 2011 OCEBM Levels rank a systematic review of randomised trials first, whereas for a treatment's benefits a current local survey ranks first.
questions.x: The best design depends on the question being asked. A prevalence question needs up-to-date data from the population in question, while a question about effects needs randomisation to rule out confounding.

questions.t: A product team keeps arguing over whether it has a "churn problem" until it agrees that churn means no login and no payment for 90 days. Now any query can settle cases, and disputes must be about the threshold. That is an operational definition.
questions.f: A product team keeps arguing over whether it has a "churn problem" until it agrees that churn means no login and no payment for 90 days. Now any query can settle cases, and disputes must be about the threshold. That is a conceptual definition.
questions.x: Defining churn by a checkable procedure lets anyone classify a customer the same way. A conceptual definition would say what churn is and why it matters, without giving a test for whether a case counts.

questions.t: Decide and justify how a staff survey will be scored before analysing the responses, since even a short questionnaire can be summed in hundreds of ways, each a potential forking path.
questions.f: Decide how a staff survey will be scored after analysing the responses, once you see which scoring fits best, since even a short questionnaire can be summed in hundreds of ways.
questions.x: Fixing the measurement rule in advance stops the choice of scoring from bending toward a wanted result. Picking the scoring that fits best after looking is the flexible, after-the-fact practice Flake and Fried warn against.

questions.t: Operationalising a concept makes claims about it checkable but doesn't make the measure right: finger length would be a perfectly reliable yet invalid measure of self-esteem.
questions.f: Operationalising a concept makes claims about it checkable but doesn't make the measure right: finger length would be a perfectly valid yet unreliable measure of self-esteem.
questions.x: Finger length gives the same reading every time, so it is reliable, but it has nothing to do with self-esteem, so it is invalid. Consistency of a measure is a different question from whether it captures the intended concept.

questions.t: The Scottish philosopher James Frederick Ferrier introduced the word "epistemology" into English in his Institutes of Metaphysic of 1854.
questions.f: The Scottish philosopher William Hamilton introduced the word "epistemology" into English in his Institutes of Metaphysic of 1854.
questions.x: Ferrier coined the English term as the first part of his Institutes, the theory of knowing. Hamilton was his friend and mentor, whose blend of Reid and Kant Ferrier later rejected.
