questions.t: Applying Ferrier's theory of ignorance to a project's list of unknowns, treat gaps that evidence could close as real ignorance, and reframe questions posed so that no answer could ever count.
questions.f: Applying Ferrier's theory of ignorance to a project's list of unknowns, treat questions posed so that no answer could ever count as the deepest ignorance, and research them first.
questions.x: For Ferrier we can be ignorant only of what could in principle be known. A gap like never having asked churned customers why they left is real ignorance; a question no evidence could settle needs rewording, not research.

questions.t: Ferrier held that whatever we know, we also know ourselves as knowing it, so the smallest unit of knowledge is the object together with the knowing subject.
questions.f: Ferrier held that whatever we know, we know independently of ourselves as knowers, so the smallest unit of knowledge is the object alone, apart from any subject.
questions.x: Ferrier's first principle is that knowing includes self-knowing, so subject and object always come together. Splitting them apart is the move he blamed for Thomas Reid's errors.

questions.t: When formalising a colleague's argument, propositional logic suffices if only "and", "or", "not" and "if" do the work; reach for predicate logic when it turns on "all", "some" or relations.
questions.f: When formalising a colleague's argument, predicate logic suffices if only "and", "or", "not" and "if" do the work; reach for propositional logic when it turns on "all", "some" or relations.
questions.x: The advice is to pick the weakest system that captures what matters. Propositional logic treats whole sentences as units, so quantifiers and relations need the extra machinery of predicate logic.

questions.t: Symbolising an argument in propositional logic loses the force of a word like "because", since whether "A because B" is true depends on more than the truth of A and B.
questions.f: Symbolising an argument in propositional logic loses the force of a word like "and", since whether "A and B" is true depends on more than the truth of A and B.
questions.x: "And" is truth-functional: "A and B" is true exactly when both parts are. "Because" also claims a connection between them, which a truth table cannot record, one of the limits of formalisation.

questions.t: George Boole recast logic as an algebra of classes in 1847 and 1854, replacing the catalogue of valid syllogisms with general procedures for arguments of any complexity.
questions.f: Gottlob Frege recast logic as an algebra of classes in 1847 and 1854, replacing the catalogue of valid syllogisms with general procedures for arguments of any complexity.
questions.x: Boole founded the algebraic tradition with his Mathematical Analysis of Logic and Laws of Thought. Frege's break came later, in 1879, with a function-argument analysis using quantifiers rather than an algebra of classes.

questions.t: To find sentences in a draft policy that can be read two ways, have several readers stop at set points and paraphrase it; anyone who restates a passage differently from your intent has found a problem.
questions.f: To find sentences in a draft policy that can be read two ways, reread it carefully yourself; if each passage reads clearly to you, it can be read only one way.
questions.x: Writers already know what they meant, so they rarely see the second parse. Paraphrase testing with real readers exposes it, because two readers restating one sentence two ways have found the ambiguity.

questions.t: An editor cuts every sentence in a leave policy to under fifteen words and declares the policy now unambiguous. That doesn't follow, because a short, easy-to-read sentence can still be read two ways.
questions.f: An editor cuts every sentence in a leave policy to under fifteen words and declares the policy now unambiguous. That follows, because a short, easy-to-read sentence can't be read two ways.
questions.x: Length isn't what creates amphiboly; a trailing modifier or an "and/or" can sit in a short sentence. That is why plain-language guidance pairs drafting rules with testing on real readers.

questions.t: Masson and Waldron (1994) found that plain-language redrafting of contracts improved non-experts' comprehension, yet comprehension stayed very low because readers misunderstood legal concepts that clashed with their beliefs.
questions.f: Masson and Waldron (1994) found that plain-language redrafting of contracts improved non-experts' comprehension to near-perfect levels, once simpler words removed the legal concepts that clashed with their beliefs.
questions.x: Simpler words and sentences helped reliably, but conceptual difficulty remained. Plain language fixes structural and word-level ambiguity, not misunderstood ideas, which is why its evidence status is mixed.

questions.t: HR studies whether a voluntary leadership course raises promotion rates, using only staff with a manager nomination, though nominations depend on both course attendance and ambition. That restriction conditions on a collider and can create a spurious link.
questions.f: HR studies whether a voluntary leadership course raises promotion rates, using only staff with a manager nomination, though nominations depend on both course attendance and ambition. That restriction blocks a confounding path and removes bias.
questions.x: The nomination is a common effect of attendance and ambition, so selecting on it opens a path between them that wasn't there. Ambition, a common cause of enrolment and promotion, is the fork that should be adjusted for instead.

questions.t: When drawing a causal diagram, justify every missing arrow, since each omitted arrow claims there is no direct effect and these are the strongest assumptions in the graph.
questions.f: When drawing a causal diagram, justify every arrow you add, since only drawn arrows make claims and a missing arrow simply leaves the question open.
questions.x: An absent arrow asserts that one variable has no direct effect on another, and those assertions decide which adjustment sets work. Drawing from subject knowledge, rather than from the variables you happen to have, keeps them honest.

questions.t: A 2021 review of 234 health studies that used causal diagrams found that only 48% reported the adjustment sets their diagrams implied, and only 21% stated their target estimand.
questions.f: A 2021 review of 234 health studies that used causal diagrams found that only 21% reported the adjustment sets their diagrams implied, and only 48% stated their target estimand.
questions.x: About half reported the adjustment set and about a fifth named the estimand, so practice lags the method's promise. When reading such a study, look for both: the question being estimated and the variables the diagram says to control.

questions.t: Renewing a software contract, a team judges two rival vendors against "what we have now", shrugging off the incumbent's known flaws while dwelling on the rivals' switching risks. That is status quo bias.
questions.f: Renewing a software contract, a team judges two rival vendors against "what we have now", shrugging off the incumbent's known flaws while dwelling on the rivals' switching risks. That is the endowment effect.
questions.x: The pull here is toward the current option over a change, with alternatives judged by their risks and the incumbent's costs left unexamined. The endowment effect is the related tendency to value an object more because you own it.

questions.t: To check a decision for status quo bias, list every option, including the current one, without marking which is the incumbent, and score them all on the same criteria.
questions.f: To check a decision for status quo bias, list the alternatives and score each one against the current option as the baseline, so the incumbent sets the standard.
questions.x: Labelling one option as the status quo is exactly what tilts choices toward it in the classic experiments. A neutral listing removes that label, while using the incumbent as the baseline builds the bias into the comparison.

questions.t: A 2021 preregistered replication found status quo bias in budget, investment and job-choice problems but not in a car-colour choice, and its authors advised against calling the bias pervasive.
questions.f: A 2021 preregistered replication found status quo bias in all four problems, car colour included, and its authors concluded the bias is pervasive across choices.
questions.x: The bias reappeared at original-sized or larger effects in three scenarios but largely vanished in the fourth. Together with the wide spread in default effects, that is why its evidence is rated mixed rather than robust.

questions.t: "If the release passed every regression test, it cannot contain a regression. It passed every test. So it is impossible for this release to contain a regression." This reasoning commits the modal scope fallacy.
questions.f: "If the release passed every regression test, it cannot contain a regression. It passed every test. So it is impossible for this release to contain a regression." This reasoning is a valid modus ponens.
questions.x: The "cannot" belongs to the whole if-then link: passing tests that would catch a regression while still containing one is what's impossible. Modus ponens licenses only "it contains no such regression", not that one was impossible.

questions.t: When someone argues from "if P, then it must be Q" and P to "Q was inevitable", grant the plain conclusion Q, then ask what separate evidence would show Q is necessary.
questions.f: When someone argues from "if P, then it must be Q" and P to "Q was inevitable", reject the conclusion Q altogether, since the invalid form shows Q is false.
questions.x: With the necessity read over the whole conditional, Q itself does follow; only the added "necessarily" is unearned. An invalid argument doesn't make its conclusion false, so the right response strips the modal rather than the claim.

questions.t: Boethius answered the worry that God's foreknowledge makes the future necessary by separating conditional necessity from simple necessity.
questions.f: Peter Abelard answered the worry that God's foreknowledge makes the future necessary by separating conditional necessity from simple necessity.
questions.x: Conditional versus simple necessity is Boethius's distinction, which medieval logicians inherited. Abelard later recast the point in his own terms, as the compound versus the divided sense of a modal statement.

questions.t: "Every invoice over the threshold needs two sign-offs. This invoice has one. So it isn't over the threshold." The conclusion is a logical consequence of the premises, whether or not the system really enforces the rule.
questions.f: "Every invoice over the threshold needs two sign-offs. This invoice has one. So it isn't over the threshold." The conclusion is not a logical consequence of the premises, because the system might not really enforce the rule.
questions.x: No situation makes both premises true and the conclusion false, so the conclusion follows. Whether the rule is enforced bears on the truth of the first premise, a separate question from the consequence relation.

questions.t: "A entails B" is a claim made about sentences, in the metalanguage, whereas "if A then B" uses a connective that builds a longer sentence within the object language.
questions.f: "If A then B" is a claim made about sentences, in the metalanguage, whereas "A entails B" uses a connective that builds a longer sentence within the object language.
questions.x: Entailment is a relation between sentences; the conditional is a piece of one sentence. Because everyday "implies" blurs the two, careful logic textbooks avoid the word.

questions.t: Tarski's 1936 paper on logical consequence picked out three marks of the ordinary notion: it is modal, it depends only on form, and it can be known a priori.
questions.f: Tarski's 1936 paper on logical consequence picked out three marks of the ordinary notion: it is modal, it depends only on form, and it can be known only through experience.
questions.x: Consequence holds necessarily, turns on logical form rather than subject matter, and needs no sensory evidence to be known. Being knowable without experience is part of what separates it from inductive support.

questions.t: Asked how long 100 analysts need for 100 files if 5 analysts review 5 files in 5 minutes, a team lead blurts "100 minutes". The right answer is 5 minutes, and 100 is the item's intuitive lure.
questions.f: Asked how long 100 analysts need for 100 files if 5 analysts review 5 files in 5 minutes, a team lead blurts "100 minutes". The right answer is 100 minutes, and 5 is the item's intuitive lure.
questions.x: Each analyst reviews one file in 5 minutes, so 100 analysts finish 100 files in the same 5 minutes. The pattern-matching "100" springs to mind first, which is exactly the kind of answer CRT items are built to tempt.

questions.t: Don't judge how reflective one job applicant is from their three-item CRT score: floor effects and limited reliability make the test better suited to comparing groups.
questions.f: Judge how reflective one job applicant is from their three-item CRT score: its free-response format makes the test reliable enough for individual decisions.
questions.x: With only three items and scores bunched at zero in naive samples, one person's score is noisy. Its research value lies in group comparisons, and prior exposure to the well-known items can raise scores further.

questions.t: Attali and Bar-Hillel (2020) found that ordinary maths items without tempting lures predicted reasoning tasks about as well as CRT items, suggesting the CRT is first of all a maths test.
questions.f: Attali and Bar-Hillel (2020) found that CRT items predicted reasoning tasks far better than ordinary maths items, confirming that the CRT measures reflection apart from maths ability.
questions.x: A single maths-ability factor fitted as well as a separate reflection factor, and the two correlated at about .90 or more. The CRT predicts well, but whether it measures reflection rather than numeracy is contested.

questions.t: A security team tests a new file-storage tool thoroughly, finds no serious flaw and concludes it is probably safe for client files. This argument from missing evidence is reasonable, since a serious flaw would very likely have shown up.
questions.f: A security team tests a new file-storage tool thoroughly, finds no serious flaw and concludes it is probably safe for client files. This argument from missing evidence is fallacious, since a lack of evidence can never count against a claim.
questions.x: What decides it is the search: a sensitive test that would probably have caught a flaw makes its silence informative. The same conclusion drawn when nobody had looked would be the fallacy.

questions.t: Told a new tool is safe because "nobody has shown it causes problems", ask what investigation was actually done and how likely it was to find a problem if one existed.
questions.f: Told a new tool is safe because "nobody has shown it causes problems", ask the sceptics to prove it unsafe, since the claim stands until someone disproves it.
questions.x: Naming the missing search exposes whether the silence means anything. Demanding that sceptics disprove the claim is the burden shift that drives the fallacy; the person proposing the change owes the evidence.

questions.t: Bid A costs 20,000 with a 60% chance of 200,000 profit; Bid B costs 40,000 with a 20% chance of 800,000, and the firm can make only one. On expected value alone B is better, though it loses money four times in five.
questions.f: Bid A costs 20,000 with a 60% chance of 200,000 profit; Bid B costs 40,000 with a 20% chance of 800,000, and the firm can make only one. On expected value alone A is better, since it wins far more often.
questions.x: A is worth 0.6 x 200,000 - 20,000 = 100,000 and B is worth 0.2 x 800,000 - 40,000 = 120,000. Expected value weighs payoffs by probability, so neither the likeliest outcome nor the biggest number should decide on its own.

questions.t: When a cost model is nonlinear, don't feed it the average input and call the result the average output, since the expectation of a function is generally not the function of the expectation.
questions.f: When a cost model is nonlinear, it's safe to feed it the average input and call the result the average output, since by linearity the expectation of a function equals the function of the expectation.
questions.x: Linearity holds for sums and for scaling or shifting a quantity, not for arbitrary functions of it. A model with thresholds or curves can give an average output far from its output at the average input.

questions.t: In Huygens's treatment of games of chance, expectation came first: his tract never uses the concept of probability, which was only later read back into it.
questions.f: In Huygens's treatment of games of chance, probability came first: his tract defined expectation from probabilities, using methods he had learned from Pascal and Fermat.
questions.x: Huygens built his method on the value of a player's expectation, a fair share of the stakes, and worked it out without learning Pascal and Fermat's methods. Probability as a concept was read into his rules afterwards.

questions.t: In Locke's dialectical version of the ad ignorantiam, a speaker demands that the opponent accept his proof or produce a better one, and Locke held that having no better one does not oblige anyone to accept it.
questions.f: In Locke's dialectical version of the ad ignorantiam, a speaker demands that the opponent accept his proof or produce a better one, and Locke held that having no better one does oblige the opponent to accept it.
questions.x: For Locke, an opponent's failure to offer a stronger proof leaves the first one exactly as strong as it was. That is the root of the modern point that not disproving a claim doesn't establish it.

questions.t: A project is $200,000 over budget; leaders can stop now or spend $150,000 on a fix with a 50% chance of recovering the overrun. While both options are judged against the original budget, prospect theory predicts they'll lean toward the gamble.
questions.f: A project is $200,000 over budget; leaders can stop now or spend $150,000 on a fix with a 50% chance of recovering the overrun. While both options are judged against the original budget, prospect theory predicts they'll lean toward stopping.
questions.x: Measured from the original budget, both options are losses, and the value function's convexity for losses makes a gamble attractive. Reframed from today's position as a new coin-flip bet, most people turn cautious, though the numbers are identical.

questions.t: A 2020 replication re-ran the original 1979 prospect theory problems with 4,098 people in 19 countries and found that 94% of the items replicated, though some effects were weaker.
questions.f: A 2020 replication re-ran the original 1979 prospect theory problems with 4,098 people in 19 countries and found that only 54% of the items replicated, with most effects much weaker.
questions.x: The core choice patterns held up across languages and countries, which is strong support for the descriptive model. The weakening and the small samples behind the 1992 parameters still mean its exact numbers shouldn't be treated as constants.

questions.t: Gal and Rucker's 2018 review argued that the evidence does not show losses to be generally more impactful than equivalent gains, and called for a more contextual account of loss aversion.
questions.f: Gal and Rucker's 2018 review argued that the evidence shows losses to be generally about twice as impactful as equivalent gains, settling the case for loss aversion.
questions.x: The review challenges prospect theory's most cited component, suggesting its popularity owes partly to the persistence of established beliefs. So the "losses loom twice as large" figure is contested, not settled.

questions.t: A day after skimming a vendor's list of made-up sample consultant names, a manager rates one of them a well-known industry expert, because the name feels familiar. Familiarity whose source has faded being taken for fame is the false fame effect.
questions.f: A day after skimming a vendor's list of made-up sample consultant names, a manager rates one of them a well-known industry expert, because the name feels familiar. Familiarity whose source has faded being taken for fame is the illusory truth effect.
questions.x: The judgment is about whether a name is famous, and it rests on familiarity whose real origin, yesterday's list, has slipped away. The illusory truth effect is the neighbouring error of rating repeated statements as more likely true.
